summary: This document defines a portion of the Management Information Base used with network management protocols. It describes managed objects for modeling the Bidirectional Forwarding Detection protocol, which quickly detects failures between two forwarding systems.

plainLanguage.summary: A dashboard on a car shows what is going on inside the engine. This RFC defines the dials for BFD, a tool that notices fast when a link between two routers breaks.

questions: how to monitor bfd with snmp
how to configure bfd with snmp
subtitle: The SNMP MIB for configuring and monitoring Bidirectional Forwarding Detection sessions on a device.

tldr.problem: Operators need a standard way to configure and monitor Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (BFD) sessions on devices from different vendors.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 7331 defines BFD-STD-MIB, with global scalars, a session table, a per-session performance table, two lookup tables and up and down notifications, using the types from RFC 7330.
tldr.outcome: Managers can create, tune and watch BFD sessions over SNMP, but the settings are sensitive and the RFC urges SNMPv3 and tight access control.

today: RFC 7331 is a Proposed Standard from August 2014 and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on the types in RFC 7330.

sections.title: Purpose and Scope
sections.content:
RFC 7331 defines a MIB module, BFD-STD-MIB, with managed objects to configure and monitor Bidirectional Forwarding Detection as specified in RFC 5880, RFC 5881, RFC 5883 and RFC 7130, for BFD versions 0 and 1. The objects are accessed through SNMP and defined in SMIv2.

The RFC does not define a compliance requirement for a system that implements only BFD version 0. It calls version 0 primarily of historical interest compared to the widespread deployment of version 1. The module reuses the types from RFC 7330 and does not re-describe BFD mechanisms already covered in the BFD RFCs.
sections.plainLanguage: BFD is a quick 'are you still there?' check between two routers. This RFC gives network tools a standard set of switches and gauges for it.

sections.title: How the MIB Is Organized
sections.content:
The module sits at { mib-2 222 } and has notifications, objects and conformance parts. The objects fall into four groups:

  • General variables: parameters global to the BFD process on the device.
  • Session table (bfdSessTable): identifies a BFD session between a pair of nodes.
  • Session performance table (bfdSessPerfTable): per-session counters, defined as an AUGMENT of the session table.
  • Mapping tables: bfdSessDiscMapTable maps a local discriminator to a session, and bfdSessIpMapTable maps interface and source and destination addresses to a session. The IP table SHOULD contain sessions of type IP.
sections.plainLanguage: It is like a school office: one sheet of rules for the whole school, a file for each student, a scorecard for each student, and two phone books to find a student by name or address.

sections.title: Global Variables
sections.content:
Four scalar objects apply to the whole BFD process:

  • bfdAdminStatus (read-write): the desired global state, one of enabled(1), disabled(2), adminDown(3) or down(4).
  • bfdOperStatus (read-only): the actual state, up(1), down(2) or adminDown(3). When it is down(2) or adminDown(3), every session MUST report the same operational status.
  • bfdNotificationsEnable: when true, the bfdSessUp and bfdSessDown notifications are emitted. The default is false.
  • bfdSessIndexNext: an unused index value for creating new session rows. A zero means no entries are available and MUST NOT be used as an index.
sections.plainLanguage: These are the master switches: turn BFD on or off for the whole device, see whether it is really working, and choose whether to get alerts.

sections.title: The Session Table
sections.content:
Each row of bfdSessTable describes one session, indexed by bfdSessIndex. Managers should read bfdSessIndexNext to get a new index when creating a row. A row holds a lot of state, which falls into a few kinds:

  • Identity: version number (0 to 7, default 1), session type, the local discriminator and the remote discriminator chosen by the other side (zero if not yet known).
  • Transport: destination and source UDP ports for control packets, the echo source UDP port, the interface, and source and destination address types and addresses. For a new session, a source port of zero lets the implementation choose its own.
  • Timing: desired minimum transmit interval, required minimum receive interval, required minimum echo receive interval and the detect multiplier, all intervals in microseconds, plus the negotiated values the local system actually uses.
  • State: administrative and operational status, the BFD session state, a diagnostic code for the last transition out of up(4), and flags such as demand mode, control-plane independence and multipoint.
  • Protection: GTSM (a TTL-based protection) with a default of true and a GTSM TTL with a default of 255.

Setting bfdSessAdminStatus to enabled(1) starts the BFD state machine for the session with an initial state of down(2). Setting it to adminDown(3) moves the session to adminDown(1) and keeps it there.
sections.plainLanguage: Each session's file lists who it talks to, how often it checks, how many missed checks it allows, and whether it is currently up or down.

sections.title: Authentication Objects
sections.content:
A session can carry authentication. The row has a flag showing whether authentication is present (default false), an authentication type (default noAuthentication), a key ID in the range -1 or 0..255 (default -1) and the key itself. The type and key use the IANA textual conventions defined in RFC 7330.

The security section calls these three objects highly sensitive and says implementers SHOULD disallow access to them.
sections.plainLanguage: If two routers use a secret password to trust each other, this is where the password settings live. They are so secret that the rules say to keep people from reading them.

sections.title: Performance Counters and Notifications
sections.content:
The performance table gives per-session counters for control packets and echo packets: packets in, out and dropped, plus timestamps of the last drop. It also tracks session up time, the last time the session went down, the last diagnostic for lost communication and how many times the session came up. Each 32-bit counter has a 64-bit high-capacity twin (names ending in HC), and the least significant 32 bits of the HC counter MUST equal the 32-bit counter. A discontinuity timestamp shows when counters were reset.

Two notifications exist: bfdSessUp and bfdSessDown. Each covers a range of contiguous session indexes that are about to enter up(4), or down(2) or adminDown(1). A device SHOULD send one notification per contiguous range to avoid a flood. For a single session, the two instance identifiers MUST be identical.
sections.plainLanguage: The scorecard counts messages sent, received and lost. When a link goes up or down, the device can ring a bell, and it rings once for a whole group of links that changed together.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
BFD can be tied into the stability of network infrastructure such as routing protocols, so an attack on a session may be very serious. Links may be declared down, or falsely declared up, with denial-of-service effects for many users.

Writable objects are sensitive. Improper changes to bfdAdminStatus or bfdSessAdminStatus can disrupt connectivity to everything reached through the affected peers, and bad changes to the interval and multiplier objects can keep connections disrupted for very long periods. Implementations SHOULD NOT allow changes to session-defining objects such as version, type, destination UDP port, multipoint flag, interface and the address objects while the session state is up(4).

The RFC states that SNMP versions before SNMPv3 did not include adequate security. It RECOMMENDS SNMPv3 with its cryptographic mechanisms, and says deploying earlier versions is NOT RECOMMENDED. The performance table may be sensitive too, depending on the environment.
sections.plainLanguage: If a stranger could flip these switches, they could make healthy links look broken. So only trusted people should be allowed to change or even read them.
